steps.title: Massive bleeding
actions: Sweep for bleeding with both hands: neck, each arm from the armpit down, then each leg from the groin down.
Apply a TQ (tourniquet) high and tight over the clothing while you are still under fire.
Apply a deliberate TQ directly to the skin 2-3 inches above the wound once you reach Tactical Field Care.
Twist the windlass until the bleeding stops and the pulse beyond the TQ is gone, then lock it in the clip.
Apply a second TQ side by side with the first if one properly applied TQ does not stop the bleeding.
Pack a groin, armpit or neck wound with a hemostatic dressing and hold firm pressure for 3 minutes.
mistakes: Self-adhering strap left slack, so the windlass cannot close the artery. Pull out all the slack before twisting.
Tourniquet laid over a joint or a cargo pocket, so the strap slips. Clear the limb and place it on flat skin above the wound.
Windlass left unsecured, so it unwinds when the casualty is moved. Lock it in the clip and fold the safety strap over it.
Chest wound packed with hemostatic gauze, which cannot reach bleeding inside the chest. Seal it instead.
steps.note: Care under fire: bleeding control only, stopped within 1 minute.

steps.title: Airway
actions: Open the mouth and remove any object you can see.
Use a head-tilt/chin-lift when nothing suggests a neck or spine injury.
Use a jaw-thrust instead when the mechanism points to a neck or spine injury.
Let a conscious casualty sit up or lean forward in whatever position keeps the airway clear.
Roll an unconscious casualty into the recovery position.
Reassess: look for chest rise, listen for moving air, feel it on your cheek.
mistakes: Blind finger sweep, which drives debris deeper and tears tissue. Remove only what you can see.
Head-tilt used after a rollover or blast, which moves a possibly broken neck. Use a jaw-thrust.
Snoring treated as sleep, so a partial obstruction is left in place. Open the airway and check again.
Recovery position used on a suspected spinal injury. Leave the casualty flat and hold the jaw forward.
steps.note: Airway work is deferred under fire; it belongs in Tactical Field Care.

steps.title: Respiration
actions: Expose the chest and sweep it with both hands for entry and exit wounds.
Roll the casualty and sweep the back before you call the torso clear.
Seal every open or sucking chest wound with a vented chest seal.
Count the breathing rate: over 20 a minute, or under 6, is respiratory distress.
Watch a sealed chest for worsening distress, which points to a tension pneumothorax.
Report any severe chest injury to medical personnel at once.
mistakes: Chest wound packed with gauze, which does nothing for bleeding inside the chest. Apply a seal.
Only the front checked, so an exit wound in the back keeps bleeding. Roll and sweep the back.
Seal applied and then forgotten, so pressure builds unseen. Reassess breathing after you seal.
Breathing judged by effort alone, so a rate of 24 a minute is missed. Count it.
steps.note: Burp or remove the seal if distress worsens after it is applied.

steps.title: Circulation
actions: Reassess every tourniquet and dressing already applied: expose the site and confirm the bleeding is stopped.
Replace a hasty tourniquet placed over the uniform with one on bare skin 2-3 inches above the wound.
Mark the application time on the tourniquet strap and on the casualty card.
Check the radial pulse and the skin: a weak or absent pulse with pale, cool, clammy skin means shock.
Treat altered mental status with no head injury as hemorrhagic shock.
Apply a pelvic binder after severe blunt or blast injury with pelvic pain, shock or a major leg amputation.
mistakes: Tourniquet time never written down, so the next level cannot judge the limb. Mark the strap and the card.
Hasty tourniquet left over the uniform, so it loosens as the fabric compresses. Convert it onto skin.
Shock called late because the radial pulse was never felt. Check it at every reassessment.
Tourniquet loosened to look at the wound, which restarts the bleeding. Expose the site without releasing it.
steps.note: Convert a tourniquet within 2 hours where bleeding can be held another way; do not remove one in place over 6 hours.

steps.title: Hypothermia
actions: Get the casualty off the cold ground onto insulating material.
Replace wet clothing with dry clothing and keep the rest of the uniform on.
Place an active warming blanket on the front of the chest and under the arms, never straight onto skin.
Enclose the casualty in an impermeable outer shell, then upgrade to an insulated system when you can.
Warm IV (intravenous) and IO (intraosseous) fluids before you run them in.
Shield the casualty from wind and rain on the evacuation platform.
mistakes: Casualty left on bare ground, which pulls heat out faster than the air does. Insulate underneath first.
Heat source laid directly on skin, which burns a casualty who cannot feel it. Keep a layer in between.
Hypothermia treated as a cold-weather problem, so a bleeding casualty on a warm day is left uncovered. Cover every major bleeder.
Uniform stripped off to search for wounds and never replaced. Expose, check, then cover again.
steps.note: Blood loss drives this cooling; it happens on warm days too.

steps.title: Pain
actions: Record a mental status check using AVPU (alert, verbal, pain, unresponsive) before you give any analgesia.
Give the CWMP (Combat Wound Medication Pack) for mild to moderate pain in a casualty still able to fight: acetaminophen 500 mg, two tablets every 8 hours, and meloxicam 15 mg once a day.
Give oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate 800 mcg for moderate pain when the casualty is not in shock or respiratory distress.
Give ketamine 20-30 mg by slow IV (intravenous) or IO (intraosseous) push when the casualty is in shock or respiratory distress.
Disarm any casualty who has been given fentanyl, ketamine or midazolam.
Keep naloxone 0.4 mg to hand whenever you use an opioid.
mistakes: Opioid given to a casualty in shock, which drops the blood pressure further. Use ketamine instead.
Weapon left on a casualty after analgesia, so a dissociated casualty is still armed. Disarm first.
Mental status never recorded before the drug, so later confusion cannot be read. Document AVPU first.
OTFC lozenge chewed, which dumps the dose at once. Tape it to a finger and keep it between cheek and gum.
steps.note: Benzodiazepines are not analgesia and are not given alongside opioids.

steps.title: Antibiotics
actions: Give antibiotics to every casualty with an open combat wound.
Give moxifloxacin 400 mg by mouth once a day when the casualty can swallow.
Give ertapenem 1 g by IV (intravenous), IO (intraosseous) or IM (intramuscular) route once a day when the casualty cannot take tablets.
Record the drug, dose, route and time on the casualty card.
mistakes: Antibiotic withheld because the wound looks clean, so a contaminated track goes untreated. Treat every open wound.
Tablets pushed on a shocked or unconscious casualty who cannot protect the airway. Use the injectable route.
Antibiotics given for burns alone, which is not an indication. Reserve them for penetrating wounds.
Dose given but never written down, so the next level repeats it or skips it. Record it on the card.
steps.note: Moxifloxacin is the tablet in the Combat Wound Medication Pack the casualty carries.

steps.title: Wounds
actions: Inspect and dress every known wound, then search the casualty again for wounds you have not found.
Cover a penetrating eye injury with a rigid eye shield over that eye only, and tape it in place.
Cover burns with dry sterile dressings and estimate the burned area to the nearest 10 percent.
Cover exposed bowel with a moist sterile dressing or a water-impermeable covering.
Leave an impaled object in place and bandage around it.
Record each wound and each dressing on the casualty card.
mistakes: Pressure patch put over an injured eye, which presses on the globe. Use a rigid shield and no pressure.
Both eyes covered for a one-sided injury, which blinds a casualty who could still move. Shield the injured eye only.
Wet dressing laid on a burn, which strips heat and drives hypothermia. Use dry sterile dressings.
Search stopped at the first wound found, so a second one keeps bleeding. Check the whole casualty.
steps.note: Treat a burned casualty as a trauma casualty with burns, not a burn casualty with injuries.

steps.title: Splinting
actions: Check the pulse, movement and sensation beyond the injury before you splint.
Splint the limb as you found it, taking in the joint above and the joint below the fracture.
Secure the splint with an elastic wrap, cravats, belts or tape.
Check the pulse, movement and sensation again once the splint is on.
Splint before you move the casualty.
mistakes: Splint tied across the fracture alone, so the limb still hinges. Take in the joint above and below.
Wrap pulled too tight, so fingers or toes turn cool, blue or numb. Loosen it and re-secure.
Circulation checked once only, so a splint that cut off the pulse goes unnoticed. Check before and after.
Casualty moved first and splinted later, which drives broken ends through tissue. Splint first.
steps.note: An injured arm can be secured to the shirt, using the sleeve as a sling.
